title: 2021 Global Semiconductor Shortage
summary: A global semiconductor shortage disrupted electronics and automotive manufacturing, causing production delays and higher technology prices worldwide. The shortage was triggered by a combination of COVID-19 pandemic disruptions, surging demand for consumer electronics during lockdowns, a fire at Renesas Electronics in Japan, drought conditions in Taiwan affecting TSMC water-dependent chip fabrication, and the US-China trade war restricting chip exports. Major automakers including Ford, GM, and Volkswagen were forced to idle factories. The shortage cost the global automotive industry an estimated $210 billion in lost revenue in 2021 alone. Lead times for some chips extended beyond 52 weeks.

Renesas Electronics factory fire in Japan (March 2021)
Taiwan drought reducing TSMC water supply
US-China trade restrictions on semiconductor exports
Automotive industry underestimating post-pandemic demand recovery
resolution_timeline: Shortage began easing in late 2022 as new fab capacity came online and demand normalized.

title: 1973 Oil Crisis
summary: The 1973 oil crisis began on October 17, 1973 when the Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries (OAPEC), led by Saudi Arabia, announced an oil embargo targeting nations that supported Israel during the Yom Kippur War, primarily the United States, the Netherlands, Portugal, Rhodesia, and South Africa. The price of oil quadrupled globally from approximately $3 per barrel to nearly $12 per barrel by early 1974. The crisis caused widespread fuel shortages, long queues at gas stations, rationing programs, and significant economic recessions across Western nations. The United States implemented the Emergency Petroleum Allocation Act and reduced highway speed limits to 55 mph to conserve fuel. The crisis accelerated interest in nuclear energy, coal, and early renewable energy research. It also exposed dangerous Western dependence on Middle Eastern oil and led to the establishment of the International Energy Agency (IEA) in 1974.

US military support for Israel
Western dependence on Middle Eastern oil
OAPEC use of oil as geopolitical leverage
resolution_timeline: The embargo was lifted on March 18, 1974 following diplomatic negotiations, but oil prices remained elevated permanently.
long_term_consequences: Establishment of the International Energy Agency (IEA) in 1974
Strategic Petroleum Reserve creation in the United States (1975)
Acceleration of North Sea oil development in UK and Norway
Increased investment in nuclear power across Western nations

title: COVID-19 Global Pandemic
summary: The COVID-19 pandemic, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus first identified in Wuhan, China in late 2019, was declared a global pandemic by the World Health Organization (WHO) on March 11, 2020. It became the most disruptive global event since World War II. Governments worldwide imposed lockdowns, border closures, and business restrictions, causing unprecedented economic contractions. Global GDP fell by approximately 3.1% in 2020, the sharpest peacetime contraction since the Great Depression. Over 7 million deaths were officially recorded globally, with excess mortality estimates suggesting significantly higher true death tolls. Supply chains across nearly every sector collapsed or were severely disrupted. Remote work became standard across knowledge industries. The pandemic triggered over $16 trillion in global fiscal stimulus. Vaccine development was accelerated through programs like Operation Warp Speed in the US, with the first mRNA vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna) authorized for emergency use within 12 months, an unprecedented scientific achievement.

title: 2022 Global Inflation Surge
summary: In 2022, global inflation reached its highest levels in four decades, driven by a combination of post-pandemic supply chain disruptions, massive fiscal stimulus spending, Russia's invasion of Ukraine driving energy and food prices sharply higher, and persistent labor market tightness. US inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022, the highest since November 1981. Eurozone inflation peaked at 10.6% in October 2022. Central banks globally responded with the most aggressive interest rate hiking cycle in decades. The US Federal Reserve raised rates from near zero to over 5.25% between March 2022 and July 2023. The Bank of England, European Central Bank, and others followed similarly aggressive paths. The rate hikes successfully reduced inflation but raised concerns about recession, triggered significant stock and bond market declines, and caused a sharp correction in housing markets. Global bond markets experienced their worst annual performance in decades in 2022.

Decade of ultra-low interest rates inflating asset prices
resolution_timeline: US inflation returned to approximately 3% by mid-2023 and approached 2% target by late 2024. Rate cutting cycles began in 2024.

title: US-China Trade War
summary: The US-China trade war began formally on July 6, 2018 when the Trump administration imposed 25% tariffs on $34 billion worth of Chinese goods under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, following an investigation concluding China engaged in unfair trade practices including intellectual property theft and forced technology transfer. China retaliated immediately with equivalent tariffs on US agricultural products, automobiles, and energy. Tariffs escalated through multiple rounds, eventually covering over $550 billion in Chinese goods and $185 billion in US goods. The conflict depressed global trade growth and accelerated supply chain diversification away from China. A partial Phase One trade deal was signed on January 15, 2020, in which China pledged to purchase an additional $200 billion in US goods over two years, though these targets were never fully met. The Biden administration largely maintained Trump-era tariffs and added new restrictions on semiconductor exports to China in October 2022.

title: 1979 Iranian Revolution and Second Oil Crisis
summary: The Iranian Revolution of 1979, which overthrew Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi and established an Islamic Republic under Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, triggered the second major oil crisis of the decade. Iran's oil production collapsed from approximately 5.5 million barrels per day to under 1 million barrels per day during the revolutionary upheaval. Global oil prices doubled from roughly $14 per barrel in 1978 to over $35 per barrel by 1980. The crisis was compounded by the outbreak of the Iran-Iraq War in September 1980, which further reduced regional output. Western nations faced severe fuel shortages, renewed rationing, and deep recessions. US President Jimmy Carter introduced the Carter Doctrine, declaring that any attempt by a foreign power to control the Persian Gulf would be considered an act of war against the United States. The crisis accelerated conservation efforts, fuel efficiency mandates, and diversification away from oil dependency across Western economies.

US support for the Shah alienating Iranian population

Iran-Iraq War outbreak (September 1980) further cutting regional supply
resolution_timeline: Oil prices began declining from 1981 as conservation measures, new production from North Sea and Alaska, and global recession reduced demand. Prices collapsed further in 1986.
long_term_consequences: Carter Doctrine reshaping US military posture in the Persian Gulf permanently
Acceleration of Alaskan and North Sea oil development
Paul Volcker's aggressive Federal Reserve interest rate policy crushing inflation but causing deep 1981-82 recession
Fuel efficiency standards dramatically tightened in US and Europe
Iran-Iraq War consuming over 1 million lives across 1980-1988

title: 2008 Global Financial Crisis
summary: The 2008 Global Financial Crisis was the most severe economic disaster since the Great Depression, triggered by the collapse of the US subprime mortgage market and the subsequent failure of major financial institutions holding trillions of dollars in mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and collateralized debt obligations (CDOs). Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on September 15, 2008 — the largest bankruptcy in US history at $639 billion in assets — triggering a global credit freeze. AIG required a $182 billion government bailout. The US Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) authorized $700 billion in financial system stabilization. Global stock markets lost approximately $30 trillion in value between 2007 and 2009. US housing prices fell approximately 30% nationally. Global trade collapsed by 12% in 2009. Unemployment in the United States reached 10% in October 2009. The crisis led to sweeping financial regulatory reform including the US Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act of 2010 and the Basel III international banking standards.

Basel III international banking capital requirements established
Zero interest rate policy (ZIRP) persisted for nearly a decade post-crisis

title: Russia's Invasion of Ukraine
summary: On February 24, 2022, Russia launched a full-scale military invasion of Ukraine, the largest land war in Europe since World War II. Russian forces attacked from multiple directions including Belarus in the north, Russia in the east, and Russian-occupied Crimea in the south. The invasion followed Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea and support for separatist forces in eastern Ukraine's Donbas region. Ukraine's armed forces, supported by Western military aid, intelligence sharing, and economic assistance, repelled the initial assault on Kyiv and launched a counteroffensive that retook significant territory in the Kharkiv region in late 2022. The conflict triggered the most extensive package of Western economic sanctions ever imposed, targeting Russian banks, oligarchs, energy exports, and the SWIFT international payments system. Russia's expulsion from SWIFT and asset freezes on the Russian central bank — totaling approximately $300 billion in frozen reserves — were unprecedented. The war caused a global energy crisis as Europe scrambled to replace Russian natural gas supplies, accelerating the clean energy transition.

Nvidia's market capitalization surpassed $1 trillion in 2023 and approached $3 trillion in 2024 as demand for its H100 GPU chips for AI training exploded. title: Paris Climate Agreement
summary: The Paris Agreement was adopted on December 12, 2015 at the 21st Conference of the Parties (COP21) of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, with 196 parties signing. It entered into force on November 4, 2016 after ratification by 55 countries representing 55% of global emissions. The agreement established a landmark global framework committing nations to hold global average temperature increase to 'well below' 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit warming to 1.5°C. Unlike the Kyoto Protocol, the Paris Agreement used Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) — voluntary national emissions targets — rather than mandatory caps, aiming for universal participation over legally binding compliance. The United States withdrew under President Trump (effective November 4, 2020) and rejoined under President Biden (January 20, 2021). Scientific assessments consistently showed that submitted NDCs were insufficient to achieve the 1.5°C target, with current trajectories pointing to approximately 2.5-3°C of warming by 2100. The agreement catalyzed massive increases in renewable energy investment, with global clean energy investment exceeding $1 trillion annually by 2023.

summary: China formally joined the World Trade Organization (WTO) on December 11, 2001, following 15 years of negotiations — the longest accession process in WTO history. China's accession was the most consequential expansion of the global trading system since the GATT's creation. Global goods prices fell dramatically, benefiting consumers but hollowing out manufacturing employment in developed nations.

title: Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Disaster
summary: On March 11, 2011, the most powerful earthquake ever recorded in Japan (magnitude 9.0) struck off the Pacific coast of Tōhoku, generating a massive tsunami with waves reaching up to 40.5 meters. title: The 1986 Chernobyl Nuclear Disaster
summary: On April 26, 1986, at 1:23 AM local time, reactor number four at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant near Pripyat in the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic suffered a catastrophic steam explosion and subsequent nuclear meltdown during a safety test conducted in violation of established procedures. The explosion and subsequent graphite fire released approximately 400 times more radiation than the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima, contaminating over 150,000 square kilometers across Soviet Ukraine, Belarus, and Russia. Approximately 350,000 people were evacuated and permanently resettled. The Soviet government initially attempted to suppress information about the disaster, delaying international notification for nearly 36 hours — the radioactive cloud was detected by Sweden's Forsmark Nuclear Power Plant on April 28. Thirty-one workers and first responders died from acute radiation syndrome directly. Long-term cancer deaths are estimated in ranges from 4,000 (WHO) to potentially tens of thousands. The Chernobyl disaster contributed significantly to the destabilization of Soviet authority and Gorbachev later cited it as a pivotal factor in his decision to pursue glasnost reforms.

title: The 2000s Housing Bubble Formation
summary: Following the dot-com bust of 2000-2002 and the September 11 attacks, the US Federal Reserve under Alan Greenspan slashed the federal funds rate from 6.5% to 1% by June 2003, where it remained through June 2004. When the Federal Reserve raised rates from 1% to 5.25% between 2004 and 2006, adjustable-rate mortgage payments became unaffordable, foreclosures surged, and housing prices began their historic collapse — eventually falling 33% nationally and triggering the 2008 global financial crisis.

title: The HIV/AIDS Global Pandemic
summary: The HIV/AIDS pandemic, first recognized in the United States in 1981 when the CDC reported unusual pneumonia cases in gay men in Los Angeles and New York, became the defining public health catastrophe of the late 20th century. The Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) was identified as the causative agent in 1983-1984 by researchers at the Institut Pasteur and the US National Cancer Institute. By the time the first effective antiretroviral therapy (AZT) was approved in 1987, the epidemic had spread globally. Sub-Saharan Africa bore by far the greatest burden — at the epidemic's peak, life expectancy in some southern African nations fell below 40 years. Globally, over 40 million people have died from AIDS-related illnesses since the epidemic's recognition. The development of Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART) in 1996 transformed HIV from a death sentence to a manageable chronic condition for those with access. The founding of UNAIDS (1996), PEPFAR (2003, committing $15 billion under President Bush), and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria (2002) represented landmark multilateral responses. Over 39 million people were living with HIV as of 2023.

title: The Black Death — Medieval Bubonic Plague Pandemic
summary: The Black Death, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis transmitted primarily via flea bites from infected rats, swept across Eurasia between 1347 and 1351, constituting the deadliest pandemic in recorded human history. The plague is believed to have originated in Central Asia and traveled westward along Silk Road trade routes, reaching Crimea in 1346, Sicily by October 1347 via Genoese trading ships, and spreading across Europe within three years. Mortality estimates range from 75 to 200 million deaths globally, with Europe losing an estimated 30-60% of its entire population in just five years. In some regions including Tuscany, Catalonia, and England, mortality reached 70-80%. The complete social, economic, and religious order of medieval society was shattered. Labor scarcity following mass death empowered surviving peasants to demand higher wages, challenging feudal economic structures and arguably contributing to the eventual decline of serfdom in Western Europe. The Church's authority was undermined by its inability to explain or prevent the catastrophe. Jewish communities were massacred across Europe as scapegoats. The plague established the concept of quarantine — derived from the Venetian quarantino (40-day isolation period).
